name: Dana Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for your time, Dana. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Riverside Motor Repairs, by the bridge, which does accident repairs and mechanical work, mostly for insurance companies. I'm on the mechanical side: suspension and steering after a crash, cooling systems, sensors behind bumpers that need resetting. I'm the junior, two years qualified, and the senior, Pete, still fixes my mistakes on the steering alignments. I love the puzzle of a crashed car, working out everything the bang has knocked out of line.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I got married in the spring to Luis, who runs his own landscaping business with two vans and three lads. We bought a house last year and both put in a lot, so the mortgage is small and we've got a good bit saved. I use AI every day: I photograph the damage and the app suggests the parts list, I use it to check repair steps, and I do Luis's invoices with it on Sunday nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a decent tool that got oversold, and that the people who use it well still get ahead. I'd say that to Pete and the lads. I'd probably share a tip or two on the garage group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be fine. People keep crashing and insurers keep paying, so accident repair work never stops, whatever AI does. I'd keep my edge from being quick with the apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd focus on getting my alignment work right so Pete stops checking it. I'd ask the owner, Mr Hale, about training on the ADAS sensors, the cameras and radars in modern bumpers, since every crash needs them reset. And I'd help Luis win a couple of bigger contracts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the routine tasks AI takes over touch your day, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. The parts list from photos already saves me half an hour per car. That just means I get more cars done, which Mr Hale likes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already on your mind, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr Hale is sixty-four and talks about selling. If a big chain buys Riverside, it'd be a different place. I've half thought about whether Luis and I could buy it ourselves.

I'd share **tips** on the garage group chat.
think: **Accident work** never stops, so I'd be fine.
I'd keep my **edge** from being quick with the apps.
do: Get her **steering alignments** right so the senior stops checking them.
Ask the owner for **sensor reset** training on modern bumpers.
Help her husband win **bigger contracts** for his landscaping firm.
S0.quote: People keep crashing and insurers keep paying, so accident repair work never stops, whatever AI does.
fieldNote: An everyday AI user who sees the **parts-from-photos** app as plain productivity.
Pre-existing thought: the **owner may sell**, and she might buy.
Her **household business** with her husband shapes her thinking.

steps.text: Keep repairing crash damage and get her alignments right
Train on resetting bumper cameras and radar sensors
Help her husband's landscaping firm win bigger contracts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a time for people who work hard and learn fast, and I wouldn't want the government getting in the way. Businesses should be free to modernise. I'd tell my friends from church the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the insurers change our garage more than the robots do. They'd use AI to price every repair from photos and squeeze every garage on cost. That hurts Mr Hale's margins, but my hands-on work stays, and I'm good with the tools, so I'd be one of the useful ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person at Riverside who handles the insurers' AI systems, since I already do it. I'd do the sensor training and an EV crash repair course. And I'd sit down seriously with Luis about buying Riverside when Mr Hale sells.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and honestly a bit ambitious. I'd see a chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for buying Riverside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our savings, a business loan, and maybe my father-in-law. He's been wanting to help Luis grow. I wouldn't take a grant to buy the garage, I'd rather owe the bank and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Riverside would struggle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, sadly. He's the best mechanic I know, but he can't stand the insurers' apps. If the work becomes half screens, he'd hate it, and he might just retire.

I'd say businesses should be **free to modernise** without government getting in the way.
think: **Insurers' AI** will squeeze garages on cost more than robots will.
My hands-on work stays, and I'm one of the **useful ones**.
do: Become the garage's go-to for **insurers' AI** systems.

Plan with her husband to **buy the garage** when the owner sells.

fieldNote: Free-market view: **no government** interference, borrow from family and bank.
Sees insurers' AI as the real force reshaping **accident repair**.
Worries for the **senior mechanic** who hates the apps.

steps.text: Handle all insurers' AI pricing systems at the garage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so families had better pull together. I'd say people should rely on each other and on their own hard work, not wait for the state. Online I'd share what I was learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think buying Riverside would be a mistake. Robots that can do crash repair would arrive around 2031, and a garage bought in 2027 would be worth very little by then. I'd be thirty, and I'd rather be in something that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd drop the buy-out idea and keep our savings. I'd stay at Riverside for the good wages, use every AI tool to be the best on the floor, and spend weekends building up Luis's business, which is outside, messy and harder for robots. We'd probably put off kids a year or two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm not scared of change, but two years is no time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why landscaping, rather than another garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every garden's different, every slope and every tree root. Luis's customers want to chat to him about their roses. I think that holds on longer than a car on a ramp.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Luis that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my husband we're not buying a garage, we're building his landscaping business instead. He'd be relieved, honestly. He never liked the idea of me owning a workshop full of debt.

I'd say people should rely on **their own work**, not wait for the state.

A garage bought now would be **worth little** by then.

steps.text: Use every AI tool to be the fastest mechanic on the floor

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for anyone who's willing. I'd tell people to learn the tools and get a second string to their bow. I'd say families and businesses should plan, not wait for handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years makes buying Riverside tempting again, but risky. AI by 2031, robots around 2034. I'd own it for maybe five or six good years. I'm not sure that's long enough to pay off a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tools every day and push for a pay rise as the garage's tech lead. I'd join Luis's business part-time from about 2031, doing his quotes and machinery. And we'd have our first child in the next couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own work looks fine for a while, but everything around me is shifting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: So you'd not buy Riverside here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Maybe a share with Pete, if he wanted, but not on my own. I'd rather put the money into Luis's vans and kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that makes you uncomfortable about your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leaving Pete and the lads, maybe. I'd be the one jumping before the garage falls, and that feels a bit disloyal to my senior mechanic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and those who work hard and learn will be fine. Government should stay out of the way. I'd say that at church and on the group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd go for it. I'd buy Riverside with Luis's dad's help, run it for eight or nine years, and bring in the robots myself when they come. I'd be forty and still in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy into Riverside around 2028, when Mr Hale sells. I'd bring in AI for estimates and bookings from day one. Around 2038 I'd look at buying robots, or sell the garage before they come. We'd have two kids by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bring in the robots yourself. Would that mean letting people go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it would, and I won't pretend otherwise. I'd try to keep Pete till he retires. A business that doesn't modernise just dies, so I'd bring the robots into my garage myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your faith shape how you'd handle that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would. I'd want to treat people fairly, give them warning and help them find something. That's what my mum would expect of me.

I'd say government should **stay out** of the way.

I'd **bring in robots** myself and still be in charge at forty.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no time to build anything. What would help is easy business loans for family firms like Luis's, so we can grow without begging for grants.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: About women in the trade. I had to work twice as hard to get a start at Riverside. If garages shrink, I'd hate for the few of us to be the first squeezed.

headlineQuote: I love the puzzle of a crashed car, working out everything the bang has knocked out of line.
portrait: Dana is a **junior mechanic** on the mechanical side of an accident repair garage.
She is **newly married** to a landscaper, with a small mortgage and good savings.
She uses **AI every day**, from parts lists to her husband's invoices.
She stays **calm** in mild pictures, turning anxious at two years.
She is **free-market** and family-minded, keen to own the garage if time allows.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to build anything.
whatWouldHelp: **Easy business loans** for family firms so they can grow without grants.
